title: You Are What You Love: The Spiritual Power of Habit
author: James K. A. Smith
target_audience: Readers interested in habits and liturgy
core_themes: The formative power of habits and practices (liturgies)
Desiring as the center of the human person
The misdirection of love in modern culture
Worship as the shaping of desire
primary_purpose: To demonstrate how our everyday habits and practices shape our desires and, consequently, our spiritual lives — arguing that true Christian spiritual formation is about transforming what we love, not just what we think or believe.

structure_format.narrative_style: Conversational, intellectual, and pastoral with storytelling elements
structure_format.organization: Divided into seven chapters including practical applications and theological exploration
features: Theological engagement with historic Christian practices

key_concepts_lessons: People are primarily defined by what they love rather than what they think or know.
Intentions alone are not enough; repeated practices (‘habits of the heart’) shape our deepest desires.
Cultural practices—‘secular liturgies’—compete with Christian worship to shape what we love.
Spiritual transformation requires intentional liturgical practices both in church and home.
Worship isn’t just expressive, but is formative: it molds our character and longings.
To be spiritually formed, one must identify and redirect loves toward God and neighbor.
notable_features: Makes Augustine’s ideas on desire relevant for contemporary readers
Emphasizes embodied, practical spirituality over mere intellectual assent
Offers practical suggestions for Christian living
Addresses contemporary cultural influences on spiritual formation
cultural_historical_context: The book responds to a contemporary Christian culture that often equates spiritual depth with information or ideas, highlighting the influence of habits and secular culture on spiritual formation. It draws on ancient Christian wisdom (especially Augustine) and applies it to modern Western life, addressing concerns about the effectiveness of traditional discipleship in an age bombarded by competing cultural ‘liturgies.’
reception_impact: Widely acclaimed in Christian circles for reorienting the focus of discipleship and spiritual formation.
Influential in church leadership and discipleship programs.
Praised for bridging the gap between scholarly theology and parish life.
Some readers challenge the high emphasis on liturgy over other aspects of discipleship.
comparable_titles: Desiring the Kingdom by James K. A. Smith
The Spirit of the Disciplines by Dallas Willard
The Divine Conspiracy by Dallas Willard
Liturgy of the Ordinary by Tish Harrison Warren
